catalog_quote: Aari has two tones, one high (H) and one low (L). Both the H and L tones can occur multiple times within the same word and there are no strict patterns for what syllables take what tones. If Aari was an accent language, it should not be possible to find more than one H tone per word, but we see words with multiple H tones in the examples below. 1. /kóná/ - dem. this 2. /qìʦéná/ - n the bread 3. /jínʦìná/ - n the boy 4. /ɡóʋáɡòʋdé/ - v beating [p. 88] ... In Hayward's (1990) description of the phonology of Aari, he classifies the language as an accent language. ... "It is clear from words uttered in isolation that there is one, but one only, high pitched syllable per word." (Hayward 1990: 439). [p. 87] ... new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (154 pp., text layer, the PDF's metadata gives the author "Marie Røsok") with extracted text at PDF pp. 35-36 and 95-98. Page mapping holds: PDF 96 = printed 87, PDF 97 = printed 88, PDF 35 = printed 26. Both quoted passages are there verbatim: printed p. 88 (§5.2.1 "Two tones: H and L") reads exactly "Aari has two tones, one high (H) and one low (L). Both the H and L tones can occur multiple times within the same word and there are no strict patterns for what syllables take what tones. If Aari was an accent language, it should not be possible to find more than one H tone per word, but we see words with multiple H tones in the examples below." followed by examples /kóná/, /qìʦéná/, /…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Røsok (the only modern primary description, Wubamer dialect) analyses Aari as a two-tone language (H, L; syllable = TBU; contour tones on the final syllable) with no strict positional pattern and makes no statement about word stress at all. The older primary source, Hayward 1990: 439 (quoted second-hand by Røsok), described a pitch accent-like system: exactly one high-pitched syllable per word, usually the final syllable in trisyllabic nouns and in consonant-final disyllabic nouns, and mostly final in vowel-final disyllabic nouns, with lexical exceptions (/wúksak/, /dóqsinti/, /barkóta/); accent placement is lexical in nouns and grammatical (paradigm-determined) in verbs.
new_statements.exceptions: Røsok: tones on nouns change under suffixation (terminal vowel lost; contour tones on marked forms); tones on verb roots vary by paradigm. Hayward (per Røsok p. 26, 87): several nouns with non-final H (/wúksak/ 'jackal', /dóqsinti/, /barkóta/).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; Hayward's observation concerns words uttered in isolation (citation forms); Røsok's data are isolated nouns plus frame sentences from one speaker of the Wubamer dialect; intonation treated separately (§5.3.4).
new_statements.identity_note: Røsok 2016 describes the Wubamer (eastern) dialect of Aari from a single speaker; Aari has ~10 dialects (Galila/Gayil in the north vs Wubamer; Glottolog separates Gayil as gayi1237 within Aari-Gayil aari1238). The dialect underlying Hayward 1990 was not verifiable from the pages opened.
